newsitem.title: FRANCE: British minister defends cloning research.
newsitem.headline: British minister defends cloning research.

text.p: A British minister on Wednesday defended controversial cloning of animals from suggestions it could lead to farmyard mutants or assembly lines of humans, predicting it would instead benefit breeding and conservation.
Junior farm minister Tony Baldry, visiting a farm show in Paris, said the first cloning of an adult sheep, announced in Britain on Sunday, had been carried out under strict control.
"The reason the work has been done is that it makes selective breeding more rapid, efficient and cost effective," Baldry told Reuters in an interview.

"It will be possible to breed livestock better adapted to changing environments more quickly than previously possible," he said, adding the same technology might also save rare zoo breeds from extinction.
French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur speculated on Tuesday the cloning research might one day spawn the science needed to produce "sheep with eight feet or chickens with six legs".
Baldry, talking beside a pen of ordinary British sheep on display at France's biggest annual agricultural event, disagreed.
"I think it is important to recognise that cloning does not add to or remove parts of the genetic material from sheep. The genetic material from cloned cell lines is intact," he said.
"In other words what you are simply doing is creating a greater number of what you already (have), so you couldn't produce what the French minister was expressing concern about."
British scientists on Sunday presented the first sheep cloned from an adult animal cell, sparking worldwide debate about what some see as a step towards human engineering.
Some commentators invoked images of duplicated dictators or human "Frankensteins".
Baldry said there was no question of this.
"This work is entirely in relation to livestock and indeed, as I think it has been made very clear, legislation prevents any similar work into humans because it is expressly forbidden."
